HTF Analysis: This is a good area to look for a reaction on the FTB because the associated FTR is significant. There is a clear decision made that price is too expensive and a resulting price cap is formed. There is a strong bearish move out of the FTR showing a significant imbalance where more orders may exist when price returns to this area. Because of these factors, I will watch the 4-hour chart until price reaches the FTR zone, at which point I will drop down to a LTF to look for specific price action to make an entry. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal 4/48 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT LTF Analysis: Price moves up through the lower limit of the FTR. Since I know price is returning for the first time, I am looking for a reason to short. Primarily, I am focused on price forming an engulf to the downside before considering any entry. I labeled the source of the engulf as the location where I would have executed a short trade. I would have placed a stop just above the upper limit of the FTR (around .78420). My target might be a little aggressive, and there's a good chance I would have taken � of the position off around .76940 just to be safe. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal 5/48 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Fakeout vs Engulf: It's my understanding that price will fakeout when IT's needs orders. Fakeouts are used to push price in to a specific zone that will contain orders. Engulfs and fakeouts both have the same effect on retail traders (tricks), but the engulf is really just indicative of future price direction. Because of this, engulfs usually don't engulf in to a significant level. That is why I think this example shows an engulf and not a F/O. My focus is on the location of the engulf and the subsequent final bullish push through the CP in to the FTR zone above (by the large black arrow). Was there a way I could have predicted that price would reach the upper FTR following the bearish engulf? I am not entirely sure how to read this chart accurately. On one hand, the engulf on the 4-hour chart could be read as a clear intention for price to drop. In this were case, the https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal 7/48 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - RTM Community IT's would need to fill lots of short orders. Since the lower FTR zone is depleted (three HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT times price has visited this FTR), it would make logical sense that price would need to find the next real level of Supply to fill short orders. The push through the CP to the upper FTR could be seen as a FTB, but it also looks like a great place to FO and load up on short orders. Maybe this is both a FTB and a FO? IF's trades often occur at levels where he experiences very little (if any) drawdown. After breaking down some of those amazing trades I notice many times he is able to predict in advance and place a PO at the exact area where price turns. I could be wrong, but it seems like he knows where the fakeouts will occur by looking left of the engulf to see what the RBD/ DBR (supply/demand) is reacting to (usually an important FTR) and determining whether there are any extreme orders left to fill in that FTR. If so, price will likely FO to a specific decision point within this FTR. That is why he often drop down to a 5 minute or 1 minute chart to plot his entry....he is looking for the most accurate decision point. This is what I need to work on because trading at these extreme levels offers the highest R:R. Maybe I am getting caught up on insignificant details (I have a tendency to obsess on details and miss the main point). Where I often struggle is stop placement - either the trades get run through or the stop gets hit just before price reverses. The difference between a winning trade and a losing trade can be stop placement. Knowing price is going to F/O allows a trader to widen their stop and keeps them on the right side of R:R. It's amazing to see how bad timing on an otherwise excellent trade setup can take a major winner and turn it in to a loser. I am actually embarrassed at https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal 31/48 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - RTM Community how often my stops get hit... HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT To improve on my past errors, I have started closely watching price to understand why price changes when it does. That's why I was surprised to see price break the extreme orders of the FTR by ten pips (AUD/USD). IF has mentioned many times that predicting a F/O should be easy. I agree that an engulf or a F/O have basically the same effect on retail traders as far as trapping them on the wrong side of the trade (and in that context the difference between them really doesn't matter). Of course, the difference between the engulf and F/O is the engulf dictates future price direction. And I would suggest (from what I know as a beginner) that it is incredibly important to distinguish between the two from a practical perspective. I suppose the other aspect of this that I need to work on is the PAZ. It seems simple enough in theory...PAZ is just the space between FTR's. For some reason, once I open a live chart, I start getting all mixed up on how to draw them, how to not leave any out, and how to understand price's reaction to them. Enough of my rambling...I really appreciate that you and D took the time to leave a comment here and I will try to stay focused on the bigger picture and get really competent at specific setups that I can duplicate over and over. Maybe I am getting caught up on insignificant details (I have a tendency to obsess on details and miss the main point). Where I often struggle is stop placement - either the trades get run through or the stop gets hit just before price reverses. The difference between a winning trade and a losing trade can be stop placement. Knowing price is going to F/O allows a trader to widen their stop and keeps them on the right side of R:R. It's amazing to see how bad timing on an otherwise excellent trade setup can take a major winner and turn it in to a loser. I am actually embarrassed at how often my stops get hit... I agree that an engulf or a F/O have basically the same effect on retail traders as far as trapping them on the wrong side of the trade (and in that context the difference between them really doesn't matter). Of course, the difference between the engulf and F/O is the engulf dictates future price direction. And I would suggest (from what I know as a beginner) that it is incredibly important to distinguish between the two from a practical perspective. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal 45/48 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - RTM Community I suppose the other aspect of this that I need to work on is the PAZ. So far, the engulf/PAZ concepts are not working out for me so I have wandered a bit off course to the Doc's Journal Here's my reasoning: I know it may not be popular to admit this here, but I am beginning to question the engulf being defined as a 'secret signal' that the institutional funds use to hint at future price directional. Of course, I say this as a humble trader who is really in the beginning stages of understanding how to trade, so I am totally open to the possibility that I am dead wrong. I mean absolutely no disrespect to anyone here, as every time I get someone to post on my Journal, I am both excited and honored. There is something very refreshing about the Doc's Journal that keeps me intrigued. He states that there are no secret signals and nobody knows where price is going to move. His strategy is simply based on S/R flip zones and watching price to find areas where https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=225 45/48 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 10 - RTM Community professional money is at work..actively accumulating positions. HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT What you see on my Journal lately is a feeble attempt at applying his lessons. Doc's philosophy is relatively straightforward and he takes the time to post step by step charts (Weekly through LTF) showing how he reads the charts and why he takes trades when he does. There are no secrets to his philosophy or ambiguity (like sometimes I find in the mainstream RTM PAZ concepts) and it is this complete (and repeated) process really helps me train my eye to see the important areas. In come cases, I have been pleasantly surprised to notice some overlapping in how the Doc and IF view the market. What IF sees as an engulf, is described by Doc as being analogous to a ice fisherman 'testing' the ice to make sure it is thick enough to support his weight. It is 'testing' that often results in the long wicked candles, and is done to test how the market will respond. A similar type of testing is the fakeout, and it manifests in a similar way ...for example (at least this is how I am understanding it) Professional money wants to move the market up, but wants to see how many bears/bulls are left in the market before doing so. I like Doc's philosophy because it offers a logical reason instead of a belief that there is a secret engulf signal for no other purposes than communicating with the institutions. I can't see a logical reason for the RTM's definition of an engulf other than it is a signal. I need to understand the logical reasons why something happens if I am going to understand how and why to trade it. The more I study, the more I think there are so many players in the market it's impossible to think there are secret signals being given. Too many different banks, governments, funds, private high net worth clients, etc... to know for sure. There are big players clashing on the open market...there has to be, right? After all, the retailers don't posses enough capital to make it worth the institutional banker's while to trick. Retailers make up a minuscule part of the market. I think even the big dogs win and lose sometimes. I agree that candlestick patterns are worthless (and the Doc touches on this many times in his Journal).It isn't so much the candle patterns (doji, evening star, etc...) as what the HTF candles are telling you about the order flow of pro money at these critical S/R levels. I am trying to think like a pro money trader "where can I enter the market at the least risk for the highest return, and who am I buying/selling to?" & "When I exit the https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=225 46/48 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 10 - RTM Community trade, who am I going to be buying/selling to?". I am such a beginner that I feel inadequate posting on here, because there are so many traders here on RTM (You, IF, RDK, Alex, Milkeyway,PTP etc...) that seem to understand these concepts and log amazing trades with consistency. Nobody can deny IF's abilities are super human and his zero draw down trades are honestly one of the most incredible things I have ever seen. The freedom one could achieve with his ability is endless For me....I am still drowning a bit, and trying to find a life jacket to keep me afloat! Thank you for your continued guidance and help Art! We always have to be aware of what price is doing in all TFs. While price can certainly move up from the point you took your trade you should realize that price is coming down from supply, and the best place to buy is at a fresh demand FTR. No matter what TF you use for entry it should be backed up by and at HTF FL/FTR. Your trade was in "no mans land" on the HTF. I certainly see your reason for the trade and it does look enticing. Price did engulf an FTR, but unfortunately it also immediately hit an important FL and the target. Its important because it is supply that engulfed and formed at the last demand. You found a place that would bounce price, but the move away from price tells you whether to keep it and discard it and try again at a better place. In this case price cp'd away which leaves no demand levels left to "guard" your entry. What you want to see is an engulf of the immediate supply/demand. Price ended up forming a QM against you. You can't see this in real time, but can see the environment in which one can form if you keep in mind all TFs and what FLs are in play on each. This is my take. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=275 30/49 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 12 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Attachments: 31/49 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=275 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 12 - RTM Community The following user(s) said Thank You: hoeschec, cuimingzhao HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU H's Trading Journal #293 hoeschec Offline Associate Trader Posts: 1795 Thank you received: 2487 HotRod wrote: Hey hoeschec here are a few things to consider regarding your loss. When price reaches one of these Supply/demand + S/R flip zones, drop down to the LTF and start marking all flags that form as price pushes up/down in to the zone. 5. Wait for an engulf of an important flag (source flag) while within the supply/demand & S/R flip zone. I think I got what you mean, just need to confirm it. thank you. peter Hi Peter, This is a relatively new concept for me, so hopefully a more experienced trader can step in and correct me if I am wrong...but here is my understanding of what I mean by 'source' engulf. When price is reaching an important HTF supply or demand zone, I drop down to a lower time frame to see how price forms as it reaches in to the area of importance. On its way in to the zone, price will FL many times (base-pole-flag...etc). FTR's will also form & I watch for these as well. What I look for is the original FL or FTR that acts as the source of the major push up in to the HTF zone. I also look for major S/R levels to mark the FTR that forms after the break of the S/R level. Basically, I want to find the FL or FTR that is important...not just FL's that form as a result of the important FL's. It is critical to find out which FL/FTR is the origin of the move in to the HTF zone because it is this FL/FTR that matters when it comes to a possible. engulf. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=300 38/46 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 13 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Previously, I would be watching the charts and point out what I thought was an engulf, when in reality all I was looking at was price breaking the high/low of a reactionary FL or (meaning nothing of importance happened). Here is a illustration I made a few pages back in my journal that I think is correct (nobody corrected me on it) and it does a decent job of illustrating this point. As you can see on the illustrated chart, the original FL/FTR (arrow 1) is the one that occurred on the very Left.This is the FL/FTR that formed after a break of an important S/R level...because of this, I would deem this FTR/FL as being important and the 'source/original' FL/FTR. You can see from this drawing that price attempts to break the original FL/FTR (arrow 2) but isn't able to. Look at Arrow 3: This arrow breaks the top limit of the RBD that formed at arrow 2 making it appear that an engulf has occurred when it hasn't. The true engulf only occurs when price is able to break the top limit of the FL/FTR show at arrow #1. The engulf happens at arrow # 4. This is confirmation that the last orders have been taken from the initial source FL/FTR and price will move to the north after (hopefully) retracing to the origin of the engulf. This is my best understanding of the concept, and although it is hard to put in to words, I hope this drawing helps. For anyone who reads this and finds flaws in my response to Peter: please let me know! I'd hate to lead another trader down the wrong path! It's a FL or FTR that served a specific HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT purpose and these FL's contain decision points that will often bounce price. That is why an engulf of these important zones is so important ... the engulf clears out those remaining orders and allows price to move freely to the next important level. Price wants the path of least resistance (I heard this quote from someone here on RTM, but I can't remember who it was that coined the phrase). Find a Base-Pole-Flag: where the Flag portion forms in a HTF supply or demand https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=350 5/49 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 15 - RTM Community zone (the HTF confirmation is very important) HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT 2. Find the high limit of the FL that formed within the HTF supply zone and watch for the area in the FL where the last orders (most extreme orders) could possibly exist. This is the MPL (I think). 7. Wait for the deep retrace to this MPL and get short with a tight stop. These entries are the ones that can be 1:10 R:R or more. A good example of this is currently AUD-USD (15M Chart). I expect price to RT to the origin of the move, however in this case (and many like it) there is quite a bit of downside that I need to cover with respect to stop placement. A single candle can have breakout traders and range traders all playing out their own views of the market price action. When price reaches an extreme, a key decision has to be made, and that really in my view comes from the larger market, with some nudging from size. If price FO's the highs, the question for the bulls is, will this hold or not. If they get any indication they could be wrong, they will close the trade - there will be a panic often at the extremes, more so in more volatile instruments. Crude is a great example. The touch trade technique can work and can be easy, as long as the math works out. I found for https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=25 38/59 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 2 - RTM Community me my ability to forecast was forever failing me. It is only made harder when you see a HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT fantastic equity curve from an academy student, whether or not that student already had excellent success before the course or not...fear and greed....it gets us all. My style is profoundly adaptive. I have learnt to read the market at the zones - that is where my market reading kicks in. Until then I merely mark areas I *think* will react. In your charts, if you only want to trade the higher timeframes then the locations you put out there are those that I would monitor, looking for key SR lines. SR helps me zone in, and then I will look for pullbacks on tick charts. Almost every pullback will get a reaction, but some will be deeper, and some will be reversals, while others will involve a stop out if you dont bother to listen to what the market is telling you. As long as you factor in MM into the process, the stop outs should be irrelevant. For me I can often get in on every reaction of a rotation in price at a key level, and I never know which one will be "the one" that will cause the best/true reversal. I factor this into my approach so that I frankly dont give a damn. I can mark the levels up in a matter of minutes, because to me my edge comes from rolling my sleeves up as price approaches them. Sr levels are debunked in the academy, but they offer a much simpler mechanism in my view. Theres nothing more disappointing than spending hours at the charts marking out all of the constructs based on the "rules", only to see all of them fail. My emotional constitution isnt mature enough for that. I would conclude with this - it is a well known fact that a method that is complex is most probably riddled with a number of emotional problems. For example, when a trader who gets off with indicators takes a big hit in the market, he/she will go in search of a better indicator that will give more edge, and they will add that to their system ad nauseum, creating a more complex system. Someone else with price aciton might create a colorful and complicated way to read price action, full of all and sundry. Most of the constructs added are products of emotional distress - loss avoidance techniques. They dont exist because they are necessary to trade, but because they offer the ability for the creator to feel less emotional pain (hope for). The cosmic joke for traders is that it is profoundly simpler than we make it out to be, often because its always about trying to avoid the innate fear of loss. Most often the person who has a complicated way of trading trades little - an phenomena I found myself doing whenever I get wrapped up in complexity. My experience now is that it is simple. I openly admit my issue is not one of price reading any longer. I struggle with the 39/59 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=25 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 2 - RTM Community emotional/psychology side and I have a coach helping. In fact I have a bit of the Jonah HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Complex going on which I never thought I would have. I mention this only to highlight that my approach is extremely simple, and when I trade now I make more money than I ever thought I could. The gravity of that has been a cause for my recent need to grow psychology....but I approach the markets extremely and profoundly simply... The more I see the harder it is to keep it all straight in 18/41 my mind. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=500 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 21 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Here is an example of how I would analyze this chart in real time (I am referring to your M1 chart and drew colored circles over the areas of interest for clarity). Yes, there is seemingly an engulf at the blue circle (as you have pointed out). Bu the only reason we see that as an engulf is because it broke the high of the FL in the orange circle. In order for an engulf to be valid, price must engulf an original FL or FTR - not simply a FL/FTR that forms as a result of a reaction to a different FL or FTR further to the left. So technically, we would have to look left to determine if the engulf was legitimate. Also, price action can form what appears to be an engulf when price is really only bouncing off a S/R flip level. This is where it gets tricky and I get confused...How could we have known the price spike shown in the black circle was a F/O and not a valid engulf to the downside? In retrospect we can decipher that it was indeed a F/O, but I'm not seeing a way to know that during the live formation of price action. The complication gets even worse when I start reviewing different time frames- it is really hard to know where to start looking since price continues to bounce and react to previous historic levels. I suppose we would have to look left and see why price engulfed to the upside in the red circle to find out if the break of that high ended in a critical location where orders were remaining. I think the engulf tends to take place in areas of low significance, whereas fake outs are essentially the IT's searching for LQ by triggering stops and finding pockets where orders reside. Sorry if this is hard to follow, I'm not good at describing this using words. One thing I didn't see in this example, which I would normally need to see, is a downside engulf prior to the fakeout. In a similar situation without compression on approach & without an engulf, it might be best to hold off on taking a TT. When did price break out of the flag that held this supply/demand? https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=625 19/31 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 26 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Watch what price does once it retraces from the original break out: If price is moving out of demand, be looking for a DBR. As you can see from this example, price turned right at this DP. I also see there is a QM level located within the DP in the Base of the DBR. Not all DP's react...even ones that occur at S/R swap levels. Often times they fail. Does this have to do with the MPL? I understand the FTR PAZ, but the other types of PAZ still confuse me and the MPL is also something I don't completely understand. It has been written many times in the RTM forums that IT's want the best possible price..Conceptually this makes sense...if I want to sell I am looking for the highest possible price to do so in order to maximize my return. Assuming I am an IT looking to short, I want to sell at the highest price possible (This is the MPL). If I am looking at a chart, there are dozens of places where I could turn price...and there will always be a supply zone or DP or FTR that exists at a price higher than current price. So when RTM traders say IT's want the best possible price, they are talking about a price level that is best within the context of the current trade setup...not necessarily the best price (hypothetically speaking, you could wait forever for price to keep climbing before shorting. There is always another level higher up). Does this question make any sense?I am not very good at describing these concepts using words. Price must defeat the bull army or the bear army before breaking out of a flag and advancing on. The decision points are the "last stand". Those flag limits are formed when an engulf happens and an FTR is formed. The FTR's that are formed are decision points and areas of true supply/demand (where price often fakes out to gather orders for liquidity). The flag contains all the PA that exists within the flag limits. The Flag is the PAZ - the portion below and above the flag/PAZ are the flag limits which "box in" the area where price bounces around until it has the ability to engulf one of the two flag limits. These flag limits represent the furthest (most extreme) set of orders remaining. This is true supply/demand (within the context of the Flag it's currently in), and this is where the MPL's are located. This is stupid question but really I don't know "what MPL is stand for"? please explain me.......!!!!!! Hi masalif, Not a stupid question. MPL stands for "Maximum Pain Level". I am probably the wrong person to ask, as I am just now beginning to understand these concepts, but I'll tell you what I currently understand the MPL to be: The MPL is the most extreme set of orders left in either of the two the Flag Limits encompassing a Flag. The Flag Limits are also FTR's and contain the true supply/demand. Price will often fake out to the MPL to grab orders to obtain maximum liquidity, so it's a good idea to learn how to draw the MPL's and anticipate a fakeout to these levels after an engulf has occurred in the opposite direction. Fakeouts: Here is a HTF chart showing a typical QM setup. I circled three critical areas that I will detail in future pictures. More detailed: https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=700 13/54 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 29 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT My explanation: These are good places to look for a low risk high return trade. I've noticed Salivan takes these frequently. I think the whole setup essentially revolves around two major pieces of PA: a fakeout followed by an engulf within the scope of a QM. For a bullish setup, we look on the higher time frames for a recent fakeout (to the downside) followed by an engulf into a PAZ (above). The fakeout forms the LL portion of the QM. The HH portion of the QM is the engulf into a PAZ above. This engulf is only valuable if it hasn't hit it's target yet. An engulf that hits it's target before retracing wouldn't be useful. Let's go back to the fakeout for second....the fakeout is where all of the detail begins for the actual entry when price returns later on. I notice there are three areas that matter within the scope price forming a fakeout: 1. The decision point where price breaks down to form the fakeout (this is an FTR, a DP, and a FL). 2. The engulf of the DP to FO (price breaks the upper level of the FL that acted as the DP for price to EG) 3. The FL that forms as a result of the engulf of the previous FL that acted as the DP for https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=700 14/54 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 29 - RTM Community price to fakeout. This new FL is the true demand and origin of the move up. It is within HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT this FL that price will bounce on return. The lowest level of this FL is the MPL and price will often fakeout to this extreme set of orders. We can anticipate this by setting an entry order with a very tight stop loss. Nice R:R. EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT There is a final engulf that occurs on the way down, prior to the fakeout. Price decides to fakeout, and price engulfs the decision to fakeout on its way back up. The engulf of the DP to FO creates a FL/FTR which is the first time significant buy orders took control. This area contains buy orders, so when price engulfs to the upside later on it returns to pick up the remaining orders. It is definitely making me think harder... Salivan and IF both are confident in the trades they take...they have tight stops with large limits. They trade in the direction of an engulf that hasn't hit its target. Trading with such tight stops requires knowing exactly where the last extreme set of orders/liquidity lies within a FL. You are right to say that we should look for trades in areas where tricks were played in the past. In every one of Salivan's trades there is a fakeout that recently occurred and his entries occur near these fakeouts. An analogy I think of: The fakeout is like a tornado that destroys a town and everyone in it. There is nothing good left for the survivors so most people pack up and leave town looking for a new place to live. A few people end up going back to this town a few days later in a last ditch effort to grab any money/gold/valuables left behind. Everyone left in such a hurry that inevitably there were some valuables left behind.These people gather up all the valuables they can find and hop on the last train leaving town. Salivan is always one of the people who go back to grab whatever valuables they can find If the point of a fakeout is to grab liquidity by trapping traders into taking the wrong position and/or triggering stop loss orders, it would make sense that a fakeout would happen in an extreme area of a FL - the extreme opposite of the engulf and target. If this is true, we can conclude that fakeouts occur in an extreme part of a flag. If a fakeout takes all liquidity in its path, it would logically make sense that no orders would be left in the area where the fakeout occurred. We know fakeouts tend to spike in to areas of liquidity - which is usually an extreme part of a FL or FTR. Maybe the goal is to look for the last place where orders exist after the fakeout has cleared out the extreme set of orders in the flag it broke in to. I would say the last fresh set of orders would be found in the extreme portion of the FL that forms after the first engulf of the base/decision to fakeout. The FL/FTR that forms after https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=775 21/54 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 32 - RTM Community the engulf of the DP to FO would be the last place for price to return to and get orders HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT before continuing on to its target. As opportunists who want to gather up value easily, we start looking around for other towns where tornadoes have recently destroyed everything. We wait for everyone to start migrating out of the town looking for a better place to live and that's when we show up to grab what is left. This is what we should be doing in these charts - looking for places where tornadoes have touched down but nobody has come back yet. Not sure if this is right though... When price moves back up and engulfs the extreme topside of Fl 1 it creates a new high, which allows us to draw a FL Box around the entire move. (See the dotted black rectangle). Since the origin of the initial move down has been engulfed to the upside (labeled as EG "A"), we can be confident the market is moving up. We should anticipate Price deeply RT to the last set of orders within the FL Box. An analogy I think of: The fakeout is like a tornado that destroys a town and everyone in it. There is nothing good left for the survivors so most people pack up and leave town looking for a new place to live. A few people end up going back to this town a few days later in a last ditch effort to grab any money/gold/valuables left behind. Everyone left in such a hurry that inevitably there were some valuables left behind.These people gather up all the valuables they can find and hop on the last train leaving town. Salivan is always one of the people who go back to grab whatever valuables they can find If the point of a fakeout is to grab liquidity by trapping traders into taking the wrong position and/or triggering stop loss orders, it would make sense that a fakeout would happen in an extreme area of a FL - the extreme opposite of the engulf and target. If this is true, we can conclude that fakeouts occur in an https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=775 48/54 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 32 - RTM Community extreme part of a flag. If a fakeout takes all liquidity in its path, it would logically HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT make sense that no orders would be left in the area where the fakeout occurred. We know fakeouts tend to spike in to areas of liquidity - which is usually an extreme part of a FL or FTR. Maybe the goal is to look for the last place where orders exist after the fakeout has cleared out the extreme set of orders in the flag it broke in to. I would say the last fresh set of orders would be found in the extreme portion of the FL that forms after the first engulf of the base/decision to fakeout. The FL/FTR that forms after the engulf of the DP to FO would be the last place for price to return to and get orders before continuing on to its target. As opportunists who want to gather up value easily, we start looking around for other towns where tornadoes have recently destroyed everything. We wait for everyone to start migrating out of the town looking for a better place to live and that's when we show up to grab what is left. This is what we should be doing in these charts - looking for places where tornadoes have touched down but nobody has come back yet. Not sure if this is right though... A engulf happens in to an area of no significance (no important OF). A fakeout has a specific purpose - to get liquidity. So fakeouts occur in to areas with substantial OF. The areas of a chart that have the most OF or liquidity is FTR's/FL's. Flag limits are also FTR's - and these areas of price structure contain important decision points. These Fl's/FTR's also represent the extreme levels of a particular flag and mark the upper/lower boundaries of price action zones (PAZ). Maybe the key to finding the best areas for a reaction/bounce is focusing more on what the initial fakeout is reacting to (look further left). Are all HH/LL in a QM a fakeout? Is it possible to have a QM form without a fakeout? Is a Diamond made up of two fakeouts? One of the HH/LL portion of the QM and another for the diamond formation (which fakeouts the initial fakeout). More diagrams - can both of these be true? If price breaks in to a PAZ it is supposed to 33/46 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=825 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 34 - RTM Community be en engulf - but what if price breaks in to a PAZ while forming a QM? Is the HH HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT portion of the QM a fakeout even through it happened in an area without important OF? QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU H's Trading Journal #900 hoeschec Offline Associate Trader Posts: 1795 Thank you received: 2487 I have been spending a lot of time trying to understand the concept behind Salivan's deep retrace. It is confusing and complicated, but I think I might be starting to understand it. Here is a chart that I found that seems to illustrate this concept. I apologize for the messy labels...they are all important in explaining the PA. I will do my best to explain (in words) what his happening in the chart. Hopefully Salivan will tell me if I am still wrong...as always, I don't want to mislead anyone here The deep retrace happens in a PAZ - between two FTR's which form the upper and lower limits of the PAZ. These FTR's also include FL's which act as the origin of the move down and the origin of the move up. If you look at the chart, you will see the origin of the move down (also target for longs). Price falls from this level, and bounces briefly before faking out (labeled fakeout # 1) below the low of the swap zone confirmation FL Box (red rectangle) where new order https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=875 49/52 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 36 - RTM Community flow was created. We identify the decision to fakeout, and wait for price to engulf this HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT DP and form a FTR/FL. This FL/FTR is also the origin of the move up, and will be the target of future shorts (this is very important to remember). Now that the origin of the move up/target for shorts is formed, we have a completed PAZ (the space between both of the origins). I labeled that in yellow. Price continues up to the origin of the move down (like Salivan says, these origins act as magnets attracting price). When price reaches this origin, it creates another fakeout to the upside (labeled fakeout # 2). Wait for price to come back down and engulf to the downside (the engulf on the chart is labeled & occurs below the blue rectangle FL Box. This engulf is important because we know the target for that engulf is the origin of the move up (it has not been hit yet, so price will be attracted to it). Price begins to fall towards the origin of the move up/ target for shorts but does not make it before reversing back to fakeout #2. Price is reversing to gather the remaining OF before continuing on to hit the target. This is good for us, because we will have a very tight stop loss and a wide target (as usual, we zoom in to find the DP to FO, and wait for an engulf of the DP to FO. The FTR/FL that forms after the EG is the best place to wait for an entry. In this case, the short was about 1:13 RR. I don't know if I am 100% correct but hopefully someone will correct me if I am wrong. The hard part will be finding these live.... but with practice it will be possible. Drawing: 1. FTR forms and Buyers are in control. Price bounces many times. 2. Price forms a RBD as it breaks the low of FTR 1. This is also the origin of the engulf 3. Engulf of 1 4. Price RT to DP to EG on its FTB 5. Price falls and a decision is made to break the low of the engulf (# 3) 6. New low is made The last decision made (5) is the origin of the last move that makes the swap zone confirmed. Until a new low is made at 6, price could have kept rising. Instead, the sellers were in control when price tested the first DP...that test is the FTB (4). Sellers are too strong and push price down to form a new low (6). Now any RT to the origin of the new low is the final DP before the confirmation of the swap zone. It is where the first level of fresh sell orders lies - true supply. Price won't fakeout above the true supply until it makes a decision to make a new swap zone. A fakeout above # 5 wouldn't net the IT's any more liquidity anyway as all the OF above # 5 was accumulated/distributed in order to form the bearish controlled swap zone. The first area where fresh order flow exists would be at #5. Is this correct? Attachments: 35/60 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=950 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 39 - RTM Community The following user(s) said Thank You: hansma, Edge, althoufx, JAVAD, Lucien HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU H's Trading Journal #965 hoeschec Offline Associate Trader Posts: 1795 Thank you received: 2487 I've been reading through Marketpedia and looking at my old posts, trying to conceptualize the MPL and true supply/demand. We know FTR's and engulfs are everywhere on a chart...there are so many of them it would be overwhelming to draw each and every FTR/FL and engulf in every time frame on the chart. We know not every engulf and FTR/FL are created equal...some are much more important than others. We focus on the most important engulfs- specifically, engulfs of established swap zones. If True supply/demand is formed after an engulf of an important swap zone, we know the true supply/demand level is also a FTR/FL. The MPL (as Jurij helped me understand with his post last night...refer to post # 953) is always located in a FTR. If everything I've said is true so far, then it makes sense that not all MPL's are created equal - some are much stronger than others. The term "MPL" isn't inherently special in any way...it isn't a 'magic' area where price won't break. It is simply the most extreme set of order flow left in a FL. The MPL is only as strong as the FTR/FL in which it resides. Not all FTR's are important, and not all FTR's will bounce price. Some FTR's are weaker than others. Similarly, not every MPL is going to hold price the way we might want. There is no guarantee an MPL will hold price at any given time. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=950 36/60 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 39 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT When price easily engulfs FL/FTR, it was able to break the MPL included within. Easy breaking of MPL = imbalance of order flow. Example - a FTR that forms after a bearish engulf that fails to hold price down doesn't have enough sell orders to compete against the buy orders that push price back up . The stronger a FL/FTR, the stronger its MPL will be. Strong MPL's will bounce price, and we can feel comfortable trading fakeouts to these MPL's. If we find critical areas where an engulf of a swap zone occurs, we can be relatively confident that the resulting formation of a FL/FTR (and the MPL included within the FTR) will be strong. Strong FTR = MPL that is likely to bounce price. MPL's that bounce price have a lot of order flow ready to protect its position. As always, I could be wrong, but I want to keep track of my thoughts. Quote: "When an opposite transaction of orders execute then price is likely to reach those orders to make LQ , this is why IF says : FOs never happen by chance" - Salivan & IF Opposite transaction of orders = swap zone Sellers in control, swaps to buyers in control buyers in control swaps to sellers in control Not all swap zones are created equal, and there isn't much in Marketpedia on identifying these zones, so I want to post a few drawings to get a better idea of which swap zones are the strongest. Like i take a circle route Hi Kutumbaba, I don't use PAZ as much as I should...to me, a PAZ is the space between FTR's or an area of compressed PA (FTR's that have all been visited by price to the MPL..leaving no more order flow. The significance of a PAZ (to me) is PAZ = lack of order flow. It is 'dead space' where price moves between two FL's. When price breaks a level and pierces a PAZ, I interpret that move as an engulf. Of course, due to fractals, there are always PAZ within PAZ within PAZ etc... as we step down in the time frame. This complicates it a bit I appreciate your post because I have limited understanding of a PAZ, and want to learn more. Target for future buys/sells This is true regardless of the scale. 1 minute chart or monthly chart...the structure and fluidity of how price moves does not change. It is the dynamic behind how orders are filled and how price moves. PA doesn't exist because we say it does, or because we name the individual components. PA forms the formations we see because that is how price moves... https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=975 19/64 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 40 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Analogy: we've all heard the comparison that the market is like a Russian 'nesting doll' (also referred to as Matryoshka Doll). It is a good analogy. Each smaller scale is nested in with the higher time frame that proceeds it. The higher the time frame, the more data is included (even if it is hard to see). We often have to drop down to lower time frames to see the details of PA on lower time frames. Every engulf/FTR/FL/PAZ/target/MPL etc.... exists in various scales within the market. As with the market, each smaller doll fits inside of a bigger doll. Assume all the dolls are put together: Even though you can't see all the individual 20/64 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=975 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 40 - RTM Community dolls when they are assembled together, you know all the individual dolls exists within HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT the largest doll. You also know (regardless of what size the doll is) the following: 1. Every doll has a head 2. Every doll has two eyes 3. Every doll has two arms 4. Every doll is painted and made of the same material etc... 5. ** You can't properly put the dolls all together without starting with the smallest doll and placing larger dolls over it consecutively. The entire doll's assemblage requires all dolls to work together** ( I am not suggesting you always start a top-down analysis by beginning on a 1-min chart, but I use this example to emphasize each part's contribution to the 'whole'. The smallest doll gets put away first, the largest doll gets assembled last (over the top of all the smaller dolls) Similar to a Russian doll, the market has its version of heads, eyes, arms, etc...Each time new orders are transacted (regardless of scale), we have a new 'doll' with fresh order flow. We know this following is also true: 1. Price engulfs to indicate future directional flow of price 2. FTR/FL formed after important engulfs are origins and future targets 3. Every engulf has a target - regardless of which scale it forms on 4. Engulfs are valid and important until its target is hit. 5. The MPL is important as last place of free order flow until price fakes out to consume the orders https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=975 21/64 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 40 - RTM Community 6. You have to pay close attention to all time frames, at all times. HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT More to follow in next post... These engulfs are valid and so are the targets...it just so happens that they are occurring within the large origin/target (PAZ) of the main original zone (labeled as "Bigger Doll A") As price bounces around in the large PAZ created between the two FL's (and two origins) of 'bigger doll A', it forms numerous RBD reactions. Salivan took the AUD-USD short trade last week, and if you refer to his chart, he writes " last pocket of demand is consumed" ...this happened after a confirmed downside engulf. (you can see the chart on his journal post # 692). That demand pocket was medium time frame origin 'up' and the future target for shorts. The shorts that pushed price in to the zone consumed the buy orders...clearing the way for price to drop down to the next target of 'Medium Doll B'. The smaller time frame targets have to be cleared before price can be free to move down and hit the original target for shorts - which originated at 'Bigger Doll A". Once a target is hit, the engulf that preceded the target is satisfied, and price can move on to take out the next closest target... once that target is hit, price can drop to the next largest target etc... Price will satisfy all the lower time frame engulfs/targets first because they have to....these smaller targets/origins were formed inside the HTF PAZ. I think this is how you can keep track of price on multiple time frames- know all of the EG's and Targets and identify them as they become satisfied. To me, its entirely dependent on the scale. For example, what looks like a FO on a smaller scale may be just a reaction to a HTF true supply/demand level, or it may be an engulf in to a new PAZ of a HTF chart. Depending on the scale, a FO may very well be a fake out...but it may also be an engulf. How we deal with the FO depends on the scale we are trading on, and what target/origin is next in line to be satisfied. Maybe it all comes down to asking "what engulf is currently in control"? The lower time frame engulfs matter more (if we are looking for exact entries and targets) because it is the LTF engulfs that have targets which will be hit first. Each engulf has: 1. Engulf 2. RT, with new Origin 3. Future target Here is a simple drawing: https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1000 37/57 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 41 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT It seems to me that every time a new engulf happens this 1-2-3 system is established. It works from the LTF out to the HTF (like the Russian stacking dolls). In order to know where to take a TT (virtually no stop loss) you have to know which engulf is in control (which 1-2-3 system is in control). As Salivan puts it, you have to ask "where is price coming from?" (at least this is my interpretation of why he asks this question.... I definitely could be wrong) This is my greatest weakness - keeping track of where the most important EG (and its associated origin/target) in relation to the entire chart. These origins and targets are important because they represent true supply/demand...which means they represent areas with free order flow. If we are going to take a trade, we have to know that there isn't any untapped area of free order flow opposite our entry (within our scale) or else, price will have a reason to take the order flow. I think this is why so many of my trades get stopped out...there is still free order flow existing in a pocket above/below my stop loss. I could be wrong through... https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1075 5/52 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 44 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Attachments: The following user(s) said Thank You: etwanm QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU H's Trading Journal #1080 hoeschec Offline Associate Trader https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1075 6/52 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 44 - RTM Community Posts: 1795 Thank you received: 2487 HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Part of the reason I asked this question is to understand how to avoid getting in on the wrong side of a trade (getting stopped out because of a fakeout). I am looking for ways to properly ID fakeouts and improve my ability to decipher the difference between an engulf and a fakeout. It isn't always clear what is a FO/EG without the benefit of hindsight. I like drawing HTF FL Boxes that form as a result of an engulf of a HTF swap zone because it narrows the PA down to a specific box, which begins with a HTF engulf. If I know where the HTF engulf is, I should be able to predict where a possible FO might occur. With that said, I think (technically) every FL Box also has an area of true supply/demand and an associated MPL. If this is the case, any FO of a FL Box would be a FO past the MPL of true supply/demand...which isn't usually supposed to happen. IF says: If the signal is given by the market mover (an engulf into a new zone), then price is very unlikely to break the extreme of the zone it just came from. So, if you have the patience to wait at the last remaining set of unfilled orders in the origin, you can be almost certain that that price will be respected. Start drawing FL Boxes - only the important ones that held price AND as https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1100 5/58 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 45 - RTM Community a result price made a new low/high. We only want the strongest zones. I found two HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT main zones: the blue rectangle shows an area of bullish/buyer control, and the long black rectangle shows an area of very strong seller control. Look how well price respects the upper level of the black rectangle....it takes a while to break this high. This is good - it means this is a strong bearish controlled zone. When price breaks this upper level, it will be significant. When looking for a target for shorts, we want to find the swap zone that gives us true demand...remember on my previous posts I said "The best place to sell is in an area that is a target for longs". It works the other way too "The best place to buy is in an area that is also a target for sells". This true demand is the origin of the move up, and it is the 'magnet' that is attracting price from above. This 'magnet attraction' concept is something Salivan came up with and it makes a lot of sense. Wait for the break of the strong bearish controlled rectangle. Here is when details matter...don't be sloppy/lazy with your analysis. Just because price breaks the upper level of the strong bear-controlled rectangle (FL Box), doesn't mean it is the best place to draw your new Fl Box. Look for the following: ** Wait for price to break your important zone. After the break, label the breaks and the https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1100 6/58 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 45 - RTM Community corresponding lows that form. HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Look at these breaks and corresponding Lows: Pick the lowest low that forms and find the high that preceded the lowest low. These two points make up you new FL Box..the important Fl Box that holds the true demand and origin of the move up. You want to choose the high the corresponds to the last low that forms because you want to origin of the move up...it has to be the last demand zone before price moves up. The chart below shows this new FL Box D. HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Now..for the most important part of this whole example: As you can see in the chart below, price broke out of FL Box C and hit the target straightaway without returning to true supply. In a situation like this, you would want to be very careful about shorting at the FTB to true supply, because the engulf has already hit its target. If you weren't aware that the target had already been hit, you might go short and place a stop above the MPL of true supply....depending on where your limit order was placed you would be stopped out (see the big red circle). Often times, I think failed trades are a result of not knowing where your target is located, after an engulf occurs. This becomes even more important when you start looking at higher time frames and drilling down on many different scales and time frames. Getting in on a trade, in the right scale, because of an engulf that has an unmet target, will drastically increase the odds that your trade works out. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1100 13/58 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 45 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Attachments: The following user(s) said Thank You: hansma, harshrthakkar, Edge, Ywicked, pfs, althoufx, kloyster32, Lucien, extraw QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU H's Trading Journal #1105 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1100 14/58 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 45 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT hoeschec Offline Associate Trader Posts: 1795 Thank you received: 2487 I will be watching this over the next 24 hours.... What would be the point of doing that, if the goal is to drop price? Only IT's have the financial power to push price on such a huge scale, and it would be a very expensive move to make to hit a DP. The only way this becomes profitable for the IT is if there are so many sell orders/liquidity/FOF in the DP above, it warrants the buying that is necessary to push price to this level. There would have to be more FOF in the DP than exists in the true supply zone below it. Sometimes it is hard to know, but it is really important because origins are also future targets. Not knowing the future target means you don't know an ORFL when you see one. Not knowing a target/ORFL = not knowing if an engulf is valid and how far price may RT before hitting the target. It can be hard to ID an origin, because often times there are multiple origins within different time scales. What process do we use to identify an origin? Generally, they occur after an engulf of an important swap zone...but there has to more to it...especially when there are multiple engulfs of swap zones all located in close proximity together (as in this EUR-AUD example. It is easy to look back in hindsight and label origins and targets, because history gives us a complete view of price reaction. The difficulty is in identifying these origins/targets in real time. I would refine that statement by adding: the difficulty is in identifying the relevant origins/targets in real time, within the proper scale of the engulf you are using to begin your trade. Every engulf has a target. Valid (actionable) engulfs have unmet targets. If every engulf has a target, we can safely assume there are many engulfs and many https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1125 9/54 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 46 - RTM Community targets all existing in relatively close proximity to each other. How do we go about HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT keeping it all straight? Here are some of my ideas on this - I have been spending a lot of time on this question because I am convinced this is the key to success in trading. Firstly: as intimidating as the issue of scale is, I think it is actually a major benefit to us traders...if we can learn how to use scale to improve and normalize our analysis. I am still very new to this, so I am also learning how to "use" scale to my benefit. Scale offers us a chance to focus on one engulf/target at a time. LTF engulfs and targets will get satisfied first (by first, I mean the lower scale time frame engulfs/targets get met before HTF targets) This happens because PA is fractal, and in order for price to move long distances to satisfy a HTF target, it must pass through countless smaller zones full of LTF engulfs and targets. This is also where the PAZ concept comes in. As confusing as the PAZ is, I think its intention is actually to simplify trading. A PAZ is defined as the space between two FTR's/FL's. Regardless of the scale, a PAZ exists between two very important decision points (the areas of true supply and true demand exist within the FTR's that contain the PAZ. In order to break out of a PAZ, price must break through one of these important FTR's. Until this happens, price will bounce around within the PAZ. How does price move out of a PAZ? I think it all goes back to FOF. Strong orders must exist to break previously important levels within a FTR. Strong orders means the bulls and bear fight it out, the team with the most liquidity wins. Breaking a strong demand zone requires ample sell orders, and breaking a strong supply zone requires ample buy orders. I am still very new to this We know the following is always true, regardless of scale: Each PAZ is bordered by a FTR/True supply/demand/associated MPL: Regardless of scale, a PAZ is only a PAZ when bordered by two controlling FTR's (one is bear controlled, the other is bull controlled). The concept of a PAZ is true in a tick chart, and it is true on a monthly chart.The only difference between a HTF PAZ and a LTF PAZ is there are a lot more subsequent PAZ's within the HTF PAZ. The PAZ's all form for the same reason, and they all break for the same reason: order flow. Analogy: the laws of gravity effect you whether you fall off a skyscraper or fall off a ladder...the only difference is how far you fall from the time you lose balance until the time you hit the ground. You pass through a lot more space on your way down from the roof of the skyscraper. There are more objects you must pass through before hitting the ground (trees, awnings, shrubs, birds, people walking along the sidewalk below, etc....) But.. the inevitable consequence of gravity is you fall & hit the ground regardless. I think the same can be said for price movement inside and throughout PAZ's. 14/54 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1125 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 46 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT In fact, a HTF chart will all of the origins and targets of various scaled (marked out with rectangles) sort of resembles a high rise building with each rectangle representing a floor of the building. Just on this TF, there are many (there are many that I didn't label also). https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1175 17/56 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 48 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT How do we go about keeping these straight? How do we assign the appropriate target for each origin? Is is based on which target is closest to the origin? Hi H, I like this question since it is all about targets. It is hard because I think there's no fixed rule. The origin is a level where an important decision was made (new transaction, new decision, FL). And to asses the importance of a DP I think we have to consider multiple things as swap zones (or S/R flips), previous FLs and symmetry (including QMs). I also think there's no fixed rule like "first engulf of a move up" because in the end what moves or holds the market are orders and if there's a wall of orders before a LTF origin FTR, price won't get there unless this barrier (important area like swap) is broken. But could be wrong, it is just what I observed from the charts. I'm coming more and more to the conclusion that there's really one origin and it is the true supply/demand FL after a swap zone break (aligned aka swapped FL). https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1175 18/56 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 48 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT But if anyone is seeing an easy fixed rule about origins then I'd love to hear about it and the way to identify it Attachments: The following user(s) said Thank You: Edge, moogroo, hoeschec, staurum "And those who were seen dancing were thought to be insane by those who could not hear the music." When trading on a live chart however, it can get very confusing. These areas have to be drawn exactly right or else the trade will fail. There is very little information on Marketpedia about these terms, and it is hard to find concrete answers for the common situations where PA is less than clear. I will start by posting some examples: Question 1: How to find and properly draw an origin I don't know of any resource on RTM that explicitly defines this. There are lots of postings with traders using origins and labeling them, but most traders are still learning and you can't just take everyone's word for it. Too often I see mistakes go unchecked in people's journals and I wonder how many novice traders are led astray by this. I know for a fact I am frequently wrong in my journal, and it bothers me to think I might be leading other traders down the wrong path. Can we come up with some concrete rules for identifying and properly drawing an origin? No abstract or vague 'half' answers but actual firm answers that we can use as the basis of all our analysis. I understand we won't be given a perfect step by step manual for how to do this, masters and associates shouldn't be asked to spoon feed us , but even a couple of verified and clearly explained pointers would be incredibly helpful. Let's start by asking how the DP and the origin of a move are related. Maybe a better question is: "with specific regard to FOF, is it the origin that makes the DP or the DP that makes the origin?" -- Every origin of a move is the beginning of price going up or down after an important engulf of a swap zone. There is a point in every single important FL Box (just prior to the rally/pole) where a decision is made to make this move. But for some reason it seems the origin and the DP are separate...but are still both equally important. What is the decision point? Isn't a decision point on a chart just represent just a specific price when the balance of buys/sells became so uneven that a major move occurs? If so, is the decision point of an origin the same regardless of what time frame/scale we are looking at? If so, we shouldn't we be able to go all the way down to a 1-min chart (or https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1175 53/56 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 48 - RTM Community lower) for every single decision point to find the exact price that represents the exact HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT moment when the decision took place? If I follow this to its logical/conceptual conclusion, wouldn't it have to be true that the origin is wherever the DP occurs? The DP is the whole reason the origin is important, right? If we can agree that the DP is what makes the origin important, and the DP is the source of the FOF that occurs at these critical levels, we have to understand that the actual fresh FOF always exists(and is formed) at a very specific point in time...we can drop down to the lowest scale possible to identify exactly when this FOF is executed. If this is all accurate, we can say true supply/demand is also located exactly at the time and price FOF is executed. * FOF/True supply/demand/origin of a move is not dependent on scale. It all exists together at a specific time and price, and finding the exact zone becomes possible the lower you look on the time frames. If everything I have written so far is accurate (and I am not sure it is) then the next logical question is..how do we go about locating this "special moment in time when FOF is born". This is where we move away from conceptual ideas and focus more on actual execution on a live chart. How does this 'magical' zone manifest itself physically on a chart? This is something I have studied a lot yet I struggle to devise a clear methodology for applying it to finding the right location for taking these types of TT. It is obvious (from all my failed trades) that we can't just trade any swap zone...even if the swap zone is formed nicely with perfectly drawn FL Boxes. The swap zone must occur in a specific location within the scope of all the PA surrounding it. It is this "elusive" location that I have yet to find. Nobody seems to directly disclose what they look for in a location to start drawing swap zones. When the question is asked, the answers are generally equivocal. This may be because answering the question of 'context' and location of swap zones exposes a great deal of the strategy behind successfully executing these types of trades. If this is true, it is good new because it means we are asking the right questions.... I may be wrong, but I think we can narrow the reasons for the failed trade at Box # 3 as a fakeout forming at circle # 7, as a reaction off something is the low represented by circle # 6. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1200 7/71 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 49 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Fakeouts occur in areas of liquidity - usually to true supply/demand. A FO always has a specific purpose. Anytime we draw swap zones and identify the DP/origin where we expect price to react, we must be sure there are no remaining pockets of FOF remaining below our entry (or above our entry if we are attempting a short trade). I have heard Salivan mention this many times in his posts. How do we go about making sure there are no pockets of FOF below or above our targeted entry? Isn't there always an area of liquidity below or above our entry if we look hard enough? The answer is yes, of course. Depending on the scale, there might be a hundred areas with FOF located somewhere above or below the targeted entry....knowing that alone doesn't help us at all. The real question is one that involves refining our definition of "areas where pockets of FOF remain". This is technically a true statement, but it is much too general and pretty unhelpful if we don't understand more context and detail. A more clever question would be: "under what specific circumstances is a pocket of FOF located above/below our targeted entry relevant with regard to a potential FO? Fakeouts aren't random - they are calculated moves to obtain liquidity. They occur all the time, but I don't think they are as random as they might seem (although I must admit they seem very random at times... ) Then there is the issue of reactive vs. original price action. Often times when we look at a chart like the USD-CHF example used in this posting, we see multiple lows and think they are all independently formed, when in reality they are often just a reaction off a different zone...it might be a reaction from a HTF area of true supply/demand but it also might just be a reaction of another reaction that is a reaction off a HTF area of true supply/demand. To complicate this further, even in a situation where price is just reacting off a different https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1200 8/71 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 49 - RTM Community level, the reaction itself is forming an independent true supply/demand level on a LTF HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT chart. It is just in a different scale. So essentially, what we have is a whole bunch of reactions off other reactions that create new reactions. All these newly created reactions include smaller areas of true supply/demand (original supply/demand that is formed independent of any reaction) and within their smaller scales price will react to these levels accordingly. All of these originally formed areas of true supply/demand have their own MPL's which dictate how far price is likely to FO. How do we know which scales are relevant and which ones are not relevant when it comes to our trade setups? Again, I repeat the question I asked above: "under what specific circumstances is a pocket of FOF located above/below our targeted entry relevant with regard to a potential FO? I think the answer to many of our failed trades can be found in answering these questions. We need to know which pockets of FOF (another way of saying this is "we need to know which areas of true supply/demand") are relevant to a possible FO occurring at our entry point. The FO takes the form of a RBD reaction to the True supply level on the left, and whether the new true supply level (true supply 2) formed by the RBD is tradeable depends on whether the FO reached the extreme set of orders (MPL) in the FL it is a reaction to. If not, a FO could still occur to MPL 1 for the remaining FOF. That would explain why only some QM setups work... every QM has a FO (the LL or HH). Whether the QM is tradeable depends on whether or not the FO reached the extreme set of orders in the FL it is reacting to (to the left). If yes, there is no need to worry about another FO...the FOF is gone from this level. The next area of FOF would occur in the FL that forms after the EG of the DP to FO...the new 'true supply' level https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1200 68/71 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 49 - RTM Community where FOF has been created. HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT It just so happens this new FOF often occurs at a the 'QM' level (more or less equal to the left shoulder of the QM) because the high of the left shoulder of a QM is where a decision is made to FO...the engulf of that important DP would occur very near to the top of that shoulder... Really incredible momentum- https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1225 26/44 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 50 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Attachments: QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU H's Trading Journal #1242 hoeschec Offline Associate Trader Posts: 1795 Thank you received: 2487 27/44 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1225 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 50 - RTM Community SomethHinOg MI hEave beeEnDnUotCicAinTgI..O.INwonder Fif OanRyUoMne else sMeeOs RthEis too: LOGOUT First, I think there is a difference between "true supply/demand (FOF) (origin up/down)" and the extreme end of a FTR that forms the edge of a FL Box. The True supply/demand doesn't always form in the FTR. We draw Fl Boxes based on the break of swap levels, therefore we draw FL boxes based on the break of FTR's. Example: This becomes important when we look to ID an engulf....are we looking for an engulf of a FL Box or an engulf of the "true supply/demand/FOF/Origin up down" within the FL Box? Both seem important... So I started looking at areas of historical charts and I noticed some of the best reactions came from areas where there was an engulf of both the origin of a move up/down (FOF) and the top/bottom of its associated FL Box. Why is this especially important? 1. The engulf of a FL Box indicates an engulf of a swap zone (and the potential forming 28/44 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1225 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 50 - RTM Community of a new opposing one) HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT 2. An engulf of Origin up/down (FOF) indicates consumption of all opposing order flow, and newly executed FOF exists as a result. We can draw lots of FL Boxes, but not every FL Box holds an important origin up/down. When an important FL Box (with an origin up/down located within it) is engulfed, the new zone formed is highly likely to react when price returns. I've noticed an EG of the origin (FOF) is followed by a FTR, but it often turns into a confirmed FL once price continues on to break the extreme of the FL Box as well, and comes back to test the FTR. This ends up looking like a DP located just under a newly formed FL Box. The big bounce happens later on, when price returns to this area, and forms a FO to the 'DP' below the new FL Box (the DP is just the FL formed after engulfing the opposing origin. While the new FL Box is important to establish a new swap zone formation, the new FOF that is formed after the engulf of the opposing origin is where all the new orders exist. When they combine, the result is a very strong level with potential to bounce price quite far. (or at least this is what i have noticed recently, as always I could be wrong ). Then, price RT a little bit before engulfing the extreme high of FL Box A (making FL Box C). We are left with two closely related FL Boxes...one created a new swap level by engulfing the opposing one (this is FL Box C) and the other engulfed opposing True Supply and is the location for newly executed FOF (Buy orders). Even though FL Box B looks like a DP below FL Box C, it is very important as the area of true FOF. When price returns later on, it bounces very strongly off the newly formed FOF - as you can see, FL Box B and FL Box C work together (like a 'special' combined FL Box) to create extra strength. This is also a ORFL... https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1225 30/44 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 50 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT And..here is a simplified version showing the special combined FL Box/ORFL & the reaction that happened when price returns to it. Answer: look left 4 times Here are the 4 important areas: I will draw each one, starting from # 4 and working my way to the reaction: https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1250 5/44 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 51 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT I start by finding true supply. Reaction is important, MPL respected. Also notice the trick. Look at the first time price engulfs the MPL of true supply...this is the start of the next FL Box. FL Box B is formed when price engulfs True Supply "A". This is also the source/DO of the FO. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1250 6/44 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 51 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Next, look for the exact candle that breaks the low of FL Box B...this is the start of a new swap zone and "True Supply" level. True Supply "C" is especially important because it formed after an engulf of a previous Decision to FO...that DP to FO was also the DP to engulf a previous TS zone (TS A). Price Reacts @ point X to the MPL of True Supply C. Point "X" is not originally formed...it was a reaction to an originally formed Supply zone. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1250 7/44 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 51 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT FL Box "D" is still Seller-controlled...the balance of power has not changed to Bulls, so this is a reaction. How do we know if we can trade the fractal TS level formed in Box D? We have to look left and see if price has already visited the MPL of the original TS zone. Reaction X has already hit the extreme set of orders in the FL contained within TS "C"...we are safe to sell when price RT to the fractal TS level created within FL Box D. That is why price reacts so nicely... The challenging part is executing the trade... (assuming a short trade setup...it would be the exact opposite for a long trade setup) The main components you must know for this trade: 1. Find an original true supply/demand zone with good history of price reaction (FL) 2. Watch for a FO above this level (RBD) 3. Draw the FL Box that forms as a result of the engulf of the original true supply zone 4. Draw the DP to FO 5. Draw the EG of the DP to FO 6. Determine the target for the EG of the DP to FO 7. If price returns to the newly created FOF (New TS) prior to hitting the target of the engulf, it is a high probability trade. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2282-h-s-trading-journal?start=1250 12/44 7/27/2018 H's Trading Journal - Page 51 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Making a mistake on any of the 7 main components above will probably result in a lost trade.
